question: How can two hands in different metres make a landscape feel motionless?
intro: A single bird calls on one high note while the lower voices turn slowly in a different metre, so the music never quite beats time. Same Lviv performance as the rest of Miroirs.

sections.label: A · The lone bird — Très lent
B · E major — the forest swells
A′ · The call returns in D minor
sections.mNote: bird’s opening call over held chords; quieter, no climax

cues.title: One bird, nothing beneath
cues.text: Marked Très lent and très doux, pianissimo, the piece opens with a single high note repeated, then a small rising-and-falling flourish. The left hand rests for the first three bars. Ravel wrote that he evoked birds lost in a dark forest in the hottest hours of summer.
cues.evidence: Scan p. 10 of the first edition shows the right hand alone with rests in the left for bars 1–3. The recording opens at its lowest level (−44.9 dB at 0:00, −38.5 dB at 0:05). Ravel’s remark from his 1928 autobiographical sketch is quoted at https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroirs_(Ravel) and at https://www.veniccio.com/blogs/news/miroirs-ravel-s-scenes-and-sketches.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A second layer enters
cues.text: Around 0:22 a lower voice begins in quiet turning figures. Ravel writes the left hand in 12/8 beneath a right hand in 4/4: each beat is divided in three below and in two above, so the right hand’s pairs of eighths fall between the left hand’s triplets.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 0:22 scores 0.61 and the level rises from −29.0 dB at 0:20 to −19.7 dB at 0:25. The simultaneous 4/4 and 12/8 are on scan p. 10 (system 2) and in the PTNA Piano Encyclopedia analysis; the entry’s exact bar is not aligned.

cues.title: For Ricardo Viñes
cues.text: Ravel dedicated Oiseaux tristes to the pianist Ricardo Viñes, whom he met in 1888. Viñes gave the first performance of Miroirs and, according to Ravel’s biographers, coined the name Apaches for their circle of friends.
cues.evidence: The dedication is listed on IMSLP’s work page. Viñes’s first meeting with Ravel in 1888 and his coining of the name Les Apaches are in Wikipedia’s Maurice Ravel article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel) and the Les Apaches article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Apaches).

cues.title: E♭ minor becomes E major
cues.text: At about a minute the key signature changes from six flats to four sharps. The top E♭ is re-spelled D♯, and the piece moves to E major. A rolled chord and the mark expressif open a brighter, fuller section in which the bird calls sound higher and louder.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:58 (0.60), after which the level and brightness climb. The 2/4 bar, double bar and new key signature are at the end of scan p. 10, and the rolled chord marked expressif opens scan p. 11. The enharmonic E♭–D♯ is described in the PTNA Piano Encyclopedia analysis.

cues.title: A loud call, a distant echo
cues.text: In this stretch a high call marked forte is answered by the same figure pianissimo, labelled lointain, far away. The left hand keeps an unbroken pattern underneath that grows faster as the section builds.
cues.evidence: Scan p. 11 shows an f call followed by the same figure marked pp and lointain. The report’s onset rate climbs from 2.0 attacks a second at 1:05 to 5.6 at 1:15, and the level dips from −11.8 dB at 1:15 to −18.6 dB at 1:20. The exact bar of the echo is not aligned.

cues.title: Press forward to the climax
cues.text: Marked mf pressez, rising chords in both hands drive the music up to forte. In this recording that is the loudest stretch of the piece, from about 1:25 to 1:35.
cues.evidence: The level jumps from −18.6 dB at 1:20 to −5.5 dB at 1:25, the two loudest windows are 1:25 and 1:30, brightness reaches 1215 Hz at 1:25 and the report has a boundary at 1:26 (0.62). The mf pressez and f markings are on scan p. 11.

cues.title: The call returns, in D minor
cues.text: The loud passage falls away. At 1:48 Ravel changes the key signature to one flat and writes pianissimo with the pedal held. The accented short–long call of the opening comes back in the right hand over tied chords. There is no second climax.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is 1:48 (1.00). The level falls from −12.9 dB at 1:35 to −25.3 dB at 1:50, the onset rate from 7.0 at 1:25 to 0.8 a second at 1:50, and the local key estimate moves to D minor by 1:55–2:00. The pp, the single flat and the returning figure are on scan p. 12.

cues.title: A first night with mixed reviews
cues.text: Viñes played Miroirs for the first time on 6 January 1906 at the Salle Érard, at a concert of the Société nationale de musique. Reviews were mixed. The programme-note writer Jane Vial Jaffe locates the novelty in harmony that avoids the home key for long stretches, with unresolved chords over pedal notes.
cues.evidence: The date, hall and society are on IMSLP’s work page. The mixed reviews and the reading of the new direction as harmonic are in Jane Vial Jaffe’s note at https://www.parlancechamberconcerts.org/individual-program-notes/maurice-ravel-(1875-1937)/the-valley-of-the-bells-for-piano, where the harmonic reading is her interpretation of Ravel’s remark, not his own account.

cues.title: A cadenza of rising runs
cues.text: Marked Lent, presque ad lib. and ppp, with the pedal down and no bar lines, slurred runs climb and fall across both hands. Ravel adds a local ritardando, then pressez légèrement. The recording’s attack rate jumps to about six a second at 2:25, the busiest moment since the climax.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundaries at 2:18 (0.47) and 2:22 (0.46) are followed by an onset rate of 5.8 a second at 2:25 and 6.6 at 2:30, against 1.2–1.6 just before. The markings, the runs and the absence of bar lines are at the top of scan p. 13.

cues.title: Not scored by Ravel
cues.text: Ravel orchestrated two of the five Miroirs, the third and the fourth, but not this one. Others have scored it: Colin Matthews made a version for the BBC Philharmonic, commissioned in 2015 for the BBC Proms, and Felix Günther arranged a simpler one, transposed down a semitone.
cues.evidence: The orchestrations are listed in Wikipedia’s Miroirs article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroirs); IMSLP’s work page records that Ravel orchestrated Nos. 3 and 4.

cues.title: Encore plus lent: home in E♭ minor
cues.text: The six flats return and Ravel marks the last bars Encore plus lent, sombre et lointain: slower, dark and distant. Slow accented figures repeat above a low pedal and thin out under perdendo. The piece ends in the E♭ minor it began in.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 3:00 (0.51) is followed by a low onset rate (0.4–1.2 a second). The 3:25 window’s strongest pitch classes are E♭, F♯ (= G♭) and B♭, an E♭ minor triad. The key signature, tempo marking and perdendo are on scan p. 13 (system 5).

cues.title: Let the sound run out
cues.text: Listen through the last fifteen seconds. Ravel marks perdendo, ppp and a fermata; in this recording the level falls to about −40 dB by 3:30 and no new attacks are detected at the end. The ending is the silence as much as the last note.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −30.7 dB at 3:20 to −36.5 dB at 3:25 and −39.5 dB at 3:30, two of the five quietest windows of the recording; the onset rate is 0.0 at 3:30. The perdendo, ppp and final fermata are on scan p. 13.

transitions.title: A short bar, then four sharps
transitions.how: The opening ends on a short 2/4 bar, and a double bar then replaces six flats with four sharps. The top E♭ of the opening motif is re-spelled as D♯, so one pitch is heard first as the tonic of E♭ minor and then as the leading note of E major. Bass and texture change at once: a rolled chord marked expressif starts the new section, and a rising bass arpeggio follows in the next bar in place of the twelve-eight rocking.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:58 (0.60), after which the level and brightness climb. The 2/4 bar, double bar, new key signature and rolled chord are on scan pp. 10–11 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693); the enharmonic reading is from the PTNA Piano Encyclopedia analysis. The exact bar line is not aligned.

transitions.title: The loudest chords drain away
transitions.how: After the forte chords the sixteenth-note drive eases. Ravel writes revenez au mouvement, the dynamic falls to piano, and a few short bars lead to a double bar with a new key signature of one flat (D minor). With the pedal held, the opening’s accented short–long call returns in the right hand above tied chords. The climax is not answered by another: the music settles into the colour it started with.
transitions.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is 1:48 (1.00). The level falls from −12.9 dB at 1:35 to −25.3 dB at 1:50, the onset rate from 7.0 a second at 1:25 to 0.8, and the key estimate settles on D minor by 1:55–2:00. Revenez au mouvement, the single flat, the pp and the returning figure are on scan p. 12. Exact bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: A short bar opens into a free cadenza
transitions.how: The D minor section thins to pianissimo bars, and a 2/4 bar ends the page. Ravel then writes Lent, presque ad lib., ppp, with the pedal down, and the next page has no bar lines: rising and falling slurred runs spread across both hands, slowed by a local ritardando and then pressed on slightly. The measured pulse gives way to a stretch where the player controls the time.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundaries at 2:18 (0.47) and 2:22 (0.46) precede an onset rate of 5.8 a second at 2:25 and 6.6 at 2:30, against 1.2–1.6 before. The 2/4 bar is at the end of scan p. 12 and the Lent, presque ad lib. markings at the top of scan p. 13. The start of the cadenza is estimated.

transitions.title: A ritardando, then au mouvement
transitions.how: The cadenza ends with a written pressez légèrement, and au mouvement restores the first pace on a new system. Three bars follow, piano, mezzo-forte, piano: a rising left-hand figure moves into a held chord beneath a short right-hand phrase. Bar lines are back, after the unbarred cadenza, and a fermata over the third chord ends the stretch.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 2:40 (0.79) follows the cadenza’s peak at 2:35; the onset rate falls from 5.4 a second at 2:35 to 2.0 at 2:40 and 0.4 at 2:55. The pressez légèrement, au mouvement and fermata are on scan p. 13 (systems 2–4). The exact bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: A fermata, then slower and darker
transitions.how: The fermata chord stops the pulse. A double bar then restores six flats, the home key of E♭ minor, and Ravel writes Encore plus lent (still slower), sombre et lointain, pianissimo. Accented figures repeat above a very low held note in the left hand, and the writing thins until perdendo and ppp. The opening’s key returns, with less sound and at a slower pace.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 3:00 (0.51) and a drop in onset rate to 0.4–1.2 a second. The 3:25 window’s strongest pitch classes (E♭, F♯, B♭) form an E♭ minor triad. The fermata, six-flat key signature, Encore plus lent and perdendo are on scan p. 13 (systems 4–5).

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
